analysis.one_liner: Lets borrowers wipe out private student loan debt in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittee until Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, bankruptcy law treats nearly all student loans as almost impossible to erase — you must prove 'undue hardship,' a very high bar. This bill would change that for private student loans only: loans from banks and other private lenders, not federal loans. People who file for bankruptcy could have their private student loans wiped out just like credit card debt or medical bills. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a floor action before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People overwhelmed by private student loan debt who file for bankruptcy. Under current law they must sue to prove 'undue hardship,' a standard few meet; under this bill their private student loans would be dischargeable like most other consumer debts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers drowning in private student loans

how_it_helps.text: Amends the federal bankruptcy code so that only government-backed or government-funded educational loans stay protected from discharge, allowing private educational loans to be erased in bankruptcy without proving undue hardship.
Strikes the provision of bankruptcy law that shielded private loans made by for-profit and private lenders, which since 2005 could not be discharged except through an undue-hardship showing.
Applies to bankruptcy cases filed on or after the law's enactment, so it would change outcomes for future filers immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders, who would lose their guarantee that borrowers cannot walk away from the debt in bankruptcy. That would likely make private student loans slightly more expensive or harder to get, since lenders price in the risk of discharge.

drawbacks.text: Private lenders would face a real loss: loans they currently collect on even from bankrupt borrowers could be erased, which could raise interest rates or tighten credit for student borrowers generally.
The bill does nothing for the much larger population of borrowers with federal student loans, which remain non-dischargeable except in cases of undue hardship.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial for a specific, often desperate group: borrowers whose private loans outlast their bankruptcy filing today and can be garnished or pursued for decades. The cost is modest and predictable — higher risk priced into private student lending, which lenders have absorbed before; private loans were dischargeable until 2005. The bill was narrow and left the bigger federal-loan problem untouched, but what it proposed was not unworkable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 6, 2013 by Rep. Steve Cohen with 14 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced.
On February 28, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — where it stayed for the remainder of the Congress.
It gathered 44 cosponsors, all Democrats, but the committee never held a markup and the House never voted on it.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and all bills not passed die at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders are better off: the protection that makes their loans nearly impossible to escape in bankruptcy survived without ever being debated. Borrowers with unpayable private loans are in the same position as before.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 44 cosponsors.

for.name: 44 of 435 House members (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 44 were Democrats.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill; it remained parked in a subcommittee for two years.

against.name: Private student loan lenders
against.role: Industry holding non-dischargeable private student loans (e.g., Sallie Mae/Nelnet)
against.what_they_did: Opposed restoring dischargeability of private student loans; lenders obtained the 2005 bankruptcy protection this bill would repeal.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 supporters (the sponsor plus 44 cosponsors) were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsors are listed, and with Republicans controlling the House and the Judiciary Committee, the bill never moved.

industries.note: The bill would strip the 2005 rule making private student loans non-dischargeable, so lenders could no longer collect from borrowers who file bankruptcy. Their protection came at the direct cost of distressed borrowers, so their interest in the bill ran against the public's.

industries.industry: For-profit colleges and private lenders' servicers
industries.note: Private loans are a funding channel for schools whose graduates often struggle to repay; easier discharge would pressure that channel. The bill did not regulate these schools directly, so the effect is indirect.
